robot-dog.title: Robot Dog
captions: Quadrupedal robot, designed and coded from scratch. The culmination of multiple leg-linkage prototypes, a full CAD assembly, and custom control code.
Inverse kinematics maps the three degrees of freedom per leg, 12 in all, to full six-degree-of-freedom control of the body.
Walks, and rotates, wiggles and gyrates smoothly, blending motion across all of its axes of freedom.

pid-seesaw.title: PID Seesaw
captions: Ball-balancing PID seesaw. An infrared sensor tracks the ball, and a servo tilts the beam to keep it balanced at the center.
Resistant to disturbances. Knock the ball away and the PID controller pulls it right back to center.

micromanipulator.title: Micromanipulator
micromanipulator.tag: Closed-loop stepper control, 100 nm theoretical resolution
micromanipulator.summary: A low-cost, 3D-printed alternative to industrial micromanipulators, which cost $1,000 to $60,000. Geometric microstepping and a magnetic-gearing encoder bring angular error down to about 0.0005°, which allows a theoretical end-effector resolution of 100 nm. Physical testing of that resolution is the next step.
captions: A DIY, $200 build of a $10,000–60,000 industrial instrument, made to move on the nanometer scale.
A new microstepping formula I derived eliminates up to 1/25 of a full step of error, 0.072°, over 140 times the precision the arm is built for.
A row of 17 axially magnetized magnets multiplies encoder resolution 8.5 times.
Closed-loop PID control holds angular error to 0.0005°, for a theoretical 100 nm resolution at the tip.

media.caption: Traditional vs. geometric microstepping
points: Standard formula: **cos θ** and **sin θ** currents, for **90°** phase spacing.
This motor's phases actually sit **45°** apart.
Modelled: the field angle ripples up to **≈0.027 rad** off target.
Geometric formula sets currents per quadrant, e.g. **cos θ − sin θ**, **√2 · sin θ**.
The field then tracks the target: **~10⁻¹⁶ rad** error.
Removes up to **1/25 of a full step** of error, in theory.

media.caption: Magnetic gearing for the encoder
points: Standard setup: one diametric magnet, **one** field turn per revolution.
Here: a row of **17** axially magnetized magnets with alternating poles.
Above the row the field rotates locally, **one full turn per magnet pair**.
The encoder sees **8.5** field turns instead of one: **8.5×** resolution.

media.caption: The magnet arc in closed loop
points: **17** magnets on the motor horn pass an **MT6835** 21‑bit encoder.
Open loop: angular error about **0.08°**.
Closed loop on encoder feedback: **0.0045°**, **18×** lower.
PID control in C++: **0.0005°**, a further **~9×**.
Theoretical end-effector resolution: **100 nm**; physical testing is next.

ship-in-a-bottle.title: Ship in a Bottle
ship-in-a-bottle.summary: A ship built from scratch and assembled inside the bottle. The work demanded extreme precision and custom tools made from clothes hangers to reach inside.

media.caption: The build: shaping and carving the hull, painting, rigging the masts and sails, then passing the folded ship through the neck and raising it inside the bottle.

chess-engine.title: Chess Engine
chess-engine.summary: A chess engine built on a bitboard representation and minimax search, later extended with iterative deepening and NNUE evaluation, which replaces handcrafted heuristics with a neural network. Rated 2000+ Elo against other bots on Lichess.

media.caption: The engine playing a game as Black.
Bitboards: the board as integers
points: **12** integers of **64 bits**, one per piece type and color.
Each bit is a square: **a1** is bit **0**, **h8** is bit **63**.
One shift and mask moves **every piece** of a type at once.
**Magic bitboards** turn sliding attacks into one table lookup.
More: [Chess Programming Wiki](https://www.chessprogramming.org/Bitboards)

media.caption: NNUE: an efficiently updatable neural network
points: Replaces handcrafted terms: material, piece tables, king safety.
Inputs are piece–square pairs; at most **32** are on.
A move flips **2–4** inputs; the first layer updates incrementally.
Small later layers keep evaluation fast on a **CPU**.
More: [Chess Programming Wiki](https://www.chessprogramming.org/NNUE)

hybrid-networks.title: EvoGrad
hybrid-networks.tag: Hybrid neural networks: NEAT with gradient descent
hybrid-networks.summary: A neural-network library where evolution designs the network and gradient descent trains it, with KAN-style learnable activation functions trained alongside the weights. On the same curve-fitting task, the learnable activations reach 500× lower error than evolution alone, in a single generation.

media.caption: Gymnasium's CartPole, solved by EvoGrad's NEAT: the fittest network of each generation of one run, all from the same start. Each reads the cart's position and velocity and the pole's angle and angular velocity, and pushes the cart left or right. Evolution adds connections, then a hidden node; by generation 4 the network balances the pole for the full 500 steps from all 100 test starts.
One target, a damped sine, fitted by EvoGrad's regression example three ways, with the same settings and seed:
points: **Evolution only:** after 300 generations the best network is still a step, with a mean squared error of 0.009.
**Plus gradient descent** on every network's weights each generation: under the 0.0002 threshold in 15 generations.
**Plus learnable activations**, Legendre expansions trained with the weights: an error of 0.000017 after one generation, from one hidden node.

media.caption: Networks evolved for XOR, sin(x) and a damped sine, each with at most three hidden nodes. Blue edges carry positive weights, red negative; thicker edges, larger weights.

tennis-simulation.title: Tennis Statistics Library
tennis-simulation.tag: Bayesian updates, Monte Carlo, live trading
tennis-simulation.summary: A library that simulates tennis matches from simple inputs, updated during play with Bayesian statistics. Monte Carlo simulation produces point importance and win probability. Tested in live trading at the 2026 US Open: positions are sized by point importance, so exposure rises ahead of the points most likely to swing the match.

media.caption: One simulated match, point by point: win probability with Bayesian serve estimates against fixed priors, and the importance of each point.
Point importance: one match, every score, and the serve.
points: **One match:** importance of each point; those above 0.1 marked by outcome, serving or receiving.
**All scores, best of 5 sets:** most points fall below 0.05; the largest reach 0.25.
**Serve:** win probability on serve falls as importance rises; the logistic fit tracks the model to about 0.5, then falls more slowly.

protein-classifier.title: Alzheimer's Protein Classifier
protein-classifier.summary: A support vector machine over genomic and proteomic data that classifies whether a protein sequence is associated with Alzheimer's disease, with controls to correct for sequence length bias. Accuracy: 80.3%.

media.caption: Accuracy and sequence length bias
points: **Fig. 2.1** Protein model: as the data shrinks to 10%, raw accuracy falls from **~89%** to **~78%**, adjusted from **~80%** to **~69%**.
**Fig. 2.2** Genome model: raw accuracy stays near **95–97%**, but adjusted accuracy is only **~50–53%**.
**Fig. 3.1** Alzheimer's-associated proteins skew shorter, peaking near **200–300** amino acids against **400–500** for the rest.
**Fig. 3.2** Non-Alzheimer's genes are dominated by a spike of **~17,000** sequences under **100** nucleotides.
Length differs between the classes, so the classifier controls for it: **80.3%** accuracy.

world-models.title: Plan Shallow While You Learn
world-models.summary: Co-authored paper accepted to the Continual World Models workshop at NeurIPS 2026 in Sydney. It shows that while a world model adapts to changed physics, planning compute should favor breadth over depth to maximize returns.

media.caption: NeurIPS 2026 · Sydney, December 12. Photo: Benh Lieu Song, CC BY-SA 4.0.
The workshop’s accepted papers include work co-authored by Yann LeCun and Fei-Fei Li. [See for yourself!](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2026/loc/sydney/workshop/137499)

Drag compresses the optimal imagination depth from H=12 to H=6 (Fig. 1). Moving the same budget from depth to refinement iterations gains +2.4 to +11.2 return across the drag tiers (Fig. 2) and leads the deep default in all six deployment panels (Fig. 3).

world-models.fullTitle: Plan Shallow While You Learn: Reallocating Planning Compute During World-Model Adaptation

asteroid-orbit.title: Orbit Determination and Photometry of the Mars-crossing Asteroid 6249 Jennifer (1991 JF1)
asteroid-orbit.summary: In a team of three, determined the orbit of asteroid 6249 Jennifer from original observations: imaging over three nights, plate solving for celestial coordinates, and computing orbital elements with the Method of Gauss. Results were written up as a technical paper, with the observations submitted to the Minor Planet Center. The paper can’t be shared publicly under the Summer Science Program’s policies.

media.caption: Left: calibrated 60-second exposure from a Las Cumbres Observatory 0.35 m telescope, with 6249 Jennifer circled. Top right: computed orbit (green) and Earth’s (blue). Bottom right: nightly photometric fits against UCAC4 reference stars.

asteroid-orbit.fullTitle: Orbit Determination and Photometry of the Mars-crossing Asteroid 6249 Jennifer (1991 JF1)
